{"id":38,"answer":"Short version: your Java notes cluster into five areas — exceptions, generics, collections (two separate comparisons), and Spring. All of this comes from your saved notes; no general knowledge was needed.

- Exceptions (id 28): checked exceptions must be declared or caught, unchecked ones are RuntimeException subclasses, and try-with-resources closes resources in reverse order.
```
try (var in = new FileInputStream(f)) {
    // in.close() runs first if a second resource is opened after it
}
```

- Generics / type erasure (id 4): List<String> becomes List at runtime, so instanceof List<String> and new T[] are both illegal, and generic varargs produce unchecked warnings.
```
if (x instanceof List<?>) { }   // legal; List<String> is not
```

- ArrayList vs LinkedList (id 3): ArrayList is array-backed so get(i) is O(1); LinkedList is O(n) for get(i) but O(1) for insert/remove at the ends. You flagged this as a pair you keep mixing up for your DSA exam.
```
list.get(0);   // ArrayList: O(1)   LinkedList: O(n)
```

- HashMap vs Hashtable (id 23): HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values and is not synchronized; Hashtable allows neither.
```
map.put(null, "v");   // HashMap: fine   Hashtable: NPE
```

- Spring (id 17): @Transactional only takes effect through the proxy, so self-invocation bypasses it — the same trap as @Cacheable.
```
this.doWork();   // bypasses @Transactional
```

So the overall shape is core Java language mechanics (exceptions, generics) plus the collections API and one framework gotcha.
